notes: \cpara{Opens the book's last post with a recap of what the author has written: untangling confused questions, telling real reasoning from fake, trying before fleeing, doing the impossible.}

\cpara{Says the techniques came from the author's own projects and may not suit everyone, points doubters to earlier posts such as the one on the conjunction fallacy, and offers, with ``I suspect,'' that understanding motivated skepticism can separate a smart person who stays smart from one who ends up stupid.}

\cpara{Lists what the art lacks: defeating akrasia, coordinating groups, instrumental rationality, training, teaching, verification, and a path to becoming an experimental science, with public relations and the gender imbalance at the edge of the list. The list is candid, and it collects points made earlier in the sequence: ``A Sense That More Is Possible'' gave the missing training and the trouble with groups, and ``3 Levels of Rationality Verification'' set out the problem of verification.}

\cpara{The post's one argument about why the art is missing: a barrier to getting started, offered as a guess. People who begin to sense that more is possible may go wrong at once, and the evidence given is David Stove on the great philosophers.}

\cfact{The attribution checks. In ``What Is Wrong with Our Thoughts?'' (in \textsc{The Plato Cult}, 1991) Stove writes of ``what the `great thinkers' really are: proper objects, indeed, of pity, but even more, of horror,'' with Hegel among the essay's main examples. The next sentence's ``by default'' is Stove's view too: ``the moment they attempt any depth or generality of thought, they go mad almost infallibly.'' The author gave the essay its own post, as promised here, on 17 May 2009; that post is not in the book.}
\cpara{Compares developing an art of thinking with the author's work on artificial intelligence: both tempt one with fake explanations of the mind and ``the amazing idea that solves everything.''}
\cpara{Claims, with ``seem like they might be,'' that the author's methods for detecting fake answers help to judge whole systems of thinking.}

\cpara{States the hope: a reader who has learned this part of the art will not go wrong at once when asking how people should think about a new problem, and will ``get a saving throw.'' It is offered as a hope.}
\cpara{Restates the guess about a barrier, with ``perhaps.''}

\cpara{Names what happens instead by default: Freudian psychoanalysis or a new religion. Freud as a founder of schools without evidence was the subject of ``Schools Proliferating Without Evidence,'' earlier in this sequence.}
\cpara{Restates the hope: that the incomplete art can get readers past the barrier, show them that an art exists, and give them a ``saving throw.''}
\cpara{Calls the hope a dream: the art of answering confused questions may be what is needed to begin the rest.}

\cpara{Leaves the task to readers, with ``Probably'': the author has other things to do and may not write up more. For information: in 2012 Julia Galef, Anna Salamon, Michael Smith and Andrew Critch founded the Center for Applied Rationality, which runs workshops of the kind the post's list calls for. Our notes on ``3 Levels of Rationality Verification'' report its 2015 study of its own workshops.}
\cpara{Announces two things to keep in mind.}

\cpara{The first: draw on many sources, not one author. The claim that no true science draws its strength from one person, and that doing so is ``an idiom of cults,'' is hedged twice with ``To the best of my knowledge.''}

\cpara{The second: the art is developed while trying to do something that matters. Here the lesson is hedged at every step (``Maybe I'm being too idealistic,'' ``I somewhat suspect,'' ``if I'm not overgeneralizing from my own history,'' ``But maybe I'm wrong'') and the alternative is named. ``Something to Protect'' (2008), earlier in the book, had stated the stronger version without a hedge: ``No one masters the Way until more than their life is at stake.''}
\cpara{Refers to ``Mandatory Secret Identities'' (8 April 2009), which is not in the book, and offers a milder slogan, ``leave the house,'' with ``perhaps I am deceived.''}

\cpara{Says the author is not sure the central rhythm of the art was ever put into words, and can give its words but not the rule that generates them, and warns that learning arcana slides by default into passwords, hymns and floating assertions.}
\cpara{Judges earlier efforts to teach the art as mostly unsuccessful and this one as a larger attempt whose effects time will tell.}
\cpara{Hopes that the site's karma system will stop the decline that the author says ended earlier communities. It refers to ``Well-Kept Gardens Die By Pacifism,'' posted two days earlier.}
\cpara{Asks readers to go forth and also return, or to do both at once, since talking to others helps keep motivation over years.}
\cpara{Closes the post and the book with the exhortation: go beyond the armchair, create new art, and report back what you learned.}
